=== 2026-04-17 TPPF Comments on Proposed Interconnection Rule.docx ===
PROJECT NO. 58481


TEXAS PUBLIC POLICY FOUNDATION'S COMMENTS ON PROPOSED 16 TAC §25.194

The Texas Public Policy Foundation (TPPF or the Foundation), through its Life:Powered initiative, respectfully submits the following comments on the proposed rule, 16 TAC §25.194, regarding interconnection standards for large loads. 

The most critical part of this rule is the structure and size of the non-refundable interconnection fee in subsection (f)(7) and how that fee may or may not reflect the costs of system upgrades that go beyond the immediate “driveway” costs associated with large loads. TPPF supports the fee but has two concerns with how the PFP structures it: (1) the value of $50,000/MW appears arbitrary and not tied to any clear cost-causation framework, and (2) directing those payments straight into the rate base dilutes the purpose of the fee, namely, to ensure recovery of project-specific interconnection costs and to protect against stranded infrastructure risk.

One way to resolve these problems would be to directly allocate the cost of the 765-kV STEP and associated projects to large loads. The Foundation’s position is that the need for the 765-kV STEP is highly uncertain and continues to request that the Commission review whether all those projects are needed and whether alternative solutions to new transmission could be employed. However, to the extent that any of those projects may be needed, the need is being driven by new large loads. While developers may argue that all consumers will receive benefits from these transmission projects and that large loads should not bear a larger share of the costs beyond their standard transmission cost of service (TCOS) uplift charges, the case for making this direct allocation is very clear. 

Our conclusion from studying similar UPlan models to what ERCOT used in its planning is that the 765-kV lines will be largely underutilized even at 140 GW of peak demand and that the lines will primarily be moving excess wind and solar generation. ERCOT’s latest projections show “base” peak demand, excluding new loads over 25 MW, remaining below 100 GW through 2032, even if consistent electric vehicle (EV) adoption in included. Medium loads (between 25 and 75 MW) comprise at most only 10-15 GW of the proposed projects beyond the base demand forecast, and adding those projects to the base would bring peak demand up to 105-110 GW in 2032. The only reason systemwide demand may rise high enough over the next 10-15 years to justify the 765-kV lines is because of loads above 75 MW.

Figures 1 and 2 show how a direct allocation of the 765-KV STEP projects to large loads would provide an enormous benefit for the rest of the consumers in ERCOT. We expect the cost of transmission apart from the 765-KV STEP to continue rising on an absolute basis (see Figure 1), but after adjusting for demand growth, the average residential ratepayer will likely see an increase in transmission charges of 30-40% over the next decade without the 765-kV STEP (see Figure 2), largely in line with inflation. However, the 765-kV STEP projects, if fully built out at the projected cost of $33 billion, would add over $3 billion to the annual systemwide TCOS, increasing residential ratepayer charges by another 50% above the baseline increase.

Figure 1
Annual Transmission Cost of Service due to CREZ Lines, Wind and Solar Interconnections, and New 765-kV Lines, Actual 2022-2024 and Estimated 2025-2034

Note: Data taken from Figure 6 in Bennett, B & Piracci, J, The explosion of transmission costs in ERCOT, Texas Public Policy Foundation, January 2026, (https://www.texaspolicy.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/2026-01-LP-Transmission-Costs-BennettPiracci.pdf).

No amount of changes to existing cost-allocation formulas can offset this specific 765-kV STEP uplift, and attempting to do so would likely lead to other negative consequences. A direct allocation of the 765-kV STEP to large loads is the most fair and simple way to finance these projects while protecting other ratepayers who will not see any net benefit from these projects. Such an allocation would also ensure that the financial risk of these projects (cost overruns, stranded infrastructure, etc.) is not borne by other ratepayers.

The other benefit of this direct allocation is that it would avoid the problems created by applying the interconnection fee toward each transmission service provider’s (TSP) rate base. If the 765-kV STEP costs are allocated apart from the normal TCOS uplift process, such that those costs never enter into each TSP’s overall rate base, then no further changes are needed to protect consumers who are supporting that rate base. Again, the cost of upgrades outside of the 765-kV STEP are not expected to reach levels that will create unbearable cost increases for ratepayers, and many of those projects will have benefits for all ratepayers that justifies their inclusion in the rate base. 

Figure 2
Annual Transmission Cost of Service uplift to an average residential ratepayer due to CREZ Lines, Wind and Solar Interconnections, and New 765-kV Lines, Actual 2022-2024 and Estimated 2025-2034

Note: The numbers in this figure were derived by normalizing the annual TCOS uplift in Figure 1 by annual system load (both historical and projected, assuming a 5% future annual increase), multiplying by the average annual residential consumption 15 MWh, and then multiplying again by 1.5 to account for the fact that residential consumers account for about 33% of load but pay about 50% of TCOS.

One clear challenge with this proposal is that it applies a fixed project cost to a set of interconnecting customers whose quantity is unknown and could vary significantly year-to-year. For example, if the ~$4 billion annual TCOS impact of the 765-kV STEP in the initial years after its completion is applied to 40 GW of interconnecting large loads, then the cost would be $100,000/MW, in line with the cost proposed by this rule. If only 4 GW of large loads interconnect in that year, the cost would be $1,000,000/MW.

First, it should be noted that this risk exists under the current regime, given that TCOS is allocated on a per MWh basis. The only difference is that the risk is spread out among all customers. Second, given that annual large load interconnections are likely to fall somewhere between 4 GW and 40 GW as the 765-kV STEP projects are being completed, the Commission could set a cap, perhaps at $250,000/MW, and pass the remaining costs for that year into the broader rate base. Finally, TPPF agrees with other commenters who have noted that any financial security imposed prior to interconnection should be refundable, so that projects are only paying for upgrades based on their final interconnection allotment.

A way to further mitigate the cost risk of the 765-kV STEP to existing ratepayers is to allocate to new generators any costs that are not covered by new large loads. Given the Commission’s goal of using the 765-kV STEP to support the interconnection of new dispatchable generation, the Foundation recommends an allocation directly to new wind and solar generators. Even if peak demand reaches a point where the 765-kV lines are more heavily utilized, that peak demand is only experienced across a few hours each year, and average demand will be 30-40% below that level. On a day-to-day basis, the primary use of these new transmission projects will be to move wind and solar around the state and to minimize congestion created by the overproduction of those resources. While any costs allocated to generators will ultimately be passed to ratepayers through higher energy prices, this allocation could help correct for a significant socialized benefit that favors diffuse wind and solar over energy dense fossil fuel and nuclear generation.

The Foundation understands that any proposal to allocate transmission costs to generators is outside the scope of this rulemaking and therefore recommends that this question be taken up either through a reconsideration of the generation interconnection cost allowance rule or through a new rulemaking that establishes a non-refundable payment for new generators, as the Alberta Energy System Operator is planning to do.

In summary, TPPF’s position is that a direct assignment of the cost of the 765-kV STEP to large loads and wind and solar generators will properly place the financial risk of these projects on the entities benefiting from them and help keep the rise in residential transmission rates reasonable. Even if cost-causation is not perfectly followed for each project, this method will produce more equitable outcomes than any attempt to manage these massive new projects with across-the-board changes to rate structures. Every decision like this will create winners and losers, and we applaud the Commission for working hard to balance many competing objectives. Taking this single step will protect existing ratepayers from dramatic cost increases while helping the Commission avoid dozens of other difficult decisions and potential unintended consequences in the future.


Sincerely,

/s/ Brent Bennett
Brent Bennett, Ph.D.
Policy Director, Life:Powered
Texas Public Policy Foundation

COMMENTS OF THE TEXAS PUBLIC POLICY FOUNDATION: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

TPPF supports the non-refundable fee proposed in subsection (f)(7) but has two concerns with how the PFP structures the fee.
The value of $50,000/MW seems arbitrary and not tied to any clear cost-causation framework.
Directing those payments straight into the rate base dilutes the purpose of the fee, which is to ensure recovery of project-specific interconnection costs and to protect against stranded infrastructure risk.
TPPF estimates that the $33 billion worth of projects being considered in the 765-kV STEP will add over $4 billion to annual TCOS in the years immediately following construction, increasing TCOS charges per consumer by nearly 50% over current levels. There is no way to allocate these costs through the current TCOS uplift process that will prevent an unreasonable increase in TCOS charges for residential ratepayers.
The need for the 765-kV STEP is highly uncertain, and the Foundation continues to request that the Commission review whether those projects are needed at all. To the extent that any of those projects are needed, ERCOT’s most recent large load forecast makes it clear that the need is driven by large loads over 75 MW. The continued overbuilding of wind and solar in the ERCOT region is also a primary driver of the need for more transmission.
The best available solution to these problems is to directly allocate the cost of the 765-kV STEP projects directly to new large loads. To avoid excessive allocations in years when large load additions may be relatively small, the allocation could be capped, perhaps at $250,000/MW. Any costs not allocated to large loads could be uplifted to the rate base or, even better, allocated to new wind and solar generators, the other primary beneficiaries of these projects.
A direct assignment of the cost of the 765-kV STEP to large loads and wind and solar generators will place the financial risk where it should lie and will keep the rise in residential transmission rates at close to the rate of inflation even if no other changes to the cost allocation formulae are enacted. Taking this single step will protect existing ratepayers from dramatic cost increases while helping the Commission avoid dozens of other difficult decisions and potential unintended consequences in the future.
